Hic modus plerumq; addicitur secundæ parti operis: lam enim aliquatenus affueuit igni lapis. Itaq; non amplius calor humidus requiritur. Veruntamen attendendum est, quod etiam in aliis locum habent sicubi fusio postulatur, nempe non violenta, sed blanda.

Quartus fundit simul & figit, nimirum & ipse in gradu secundo, sed moræ longioris. Quod enim prius est fusum (exemplo fit alumen, vel atramentum, vel nitrum) id perseuerante igne eodem figitur. Quintus modus est calidi ficei gradu tertio, cuius effectum extra fusionem calcinare. Res enim quæ hoc igni tractatur, iam fixa est, quodammodo, nec debet fundi, sed sensim exiccari inque calcem redigi. Intelligunt tamen Philosophi non semper actualem calcis effectionem, sed talem laborem igneinque, quali alias calcinatur plumbum, lapis vel similia. Itaque & calx vocatur tunc lapis, licet lacis plebeiæ nullam formam habeat. Aurum & argentum, funderet ille modus: sed non lapidem. Igni follium, quem septimum numerant, itidem violente fundimus, proflamus, separamus. Itaq; non erit gradu inferiore. Eo nonnunquam flores antimonii facimus. Octauus parumi differt à septimo. Procedit faltem eius operatio per fusionem ad calcem.

Therefore, after we dissolve in the first grade, we coagulate in the second, with humidity dominating in the former and dryness in the latter. Thus, those who have also dissolved and separated essences in other arts through digestion in a bath or manure, after they have purified and exalted them, unite them in turn with dry heat, which they attribute to ashes. For this reason, Lull’s <note>referring to Ramon Llull, the Majorcan philosopher and alchemist</note> short clause expressly names the heat of the bath and ashes in the preparation of the Philosopher’s Stone, namely, the dissolving and coagulating heat.

The third mode of fire, warm and dry in the second grade, is equated to the heat of an oven that is left after the bread is extracted, and it is said to melt gently without combustion. This mode is mostly assigned to the second part of the work, for the stone has now become accustomed to fire to some extent. Therefore, moist heat is no longer required. However, it must be noted that it also has a place in other areas where fusion is requested, namely not violent, but mild.

The fourth melts and fixes at the same time, namely itself in the second grade, but of a longer duration. For that which has been melted first (for example, alum, or vitriol, or saltpeter) is fixed by the same fire persisting. Hence, after the imbibition of the stone, as we proceed with coagulating, we finally fix the spirits, indeed in the same grade, but varied according to the beginning, middle, and end.

The fifth mode is that of warm, dry heat in the third grade, the effect of which is to calcine, apart from fusion. For the thing treated with this fire is already fixed in a way, and ought not to be melted, but slowly dried and reduced to <term>calx</term> <gloss>powdered oxide</gloss>. The Philosophers, however, do not always mean the actual creation of lime, but such labor and fire as that by which lead, stone, or similar things are otherwise calcined. Thus, the stone is then also called lime, although it has no form of common lime. That mode would melt gold and silver, but not the stone. A calcining furnace is assigned to it, since the thing can be done in the same vessel.

The sixth is defined by the fourth grade of heat and dryness, and is said to melt violently or strongly. Here it is fitting to know that with the third grade persisting and being duly applied, the humidity is gradually absorbed so that no fusion occurs: but this mode dissolves the lime made in that way by the strength of heat. Imagine antimony gradually reduced to lime without liquefaction in the third grade. That lime is melted by the incoming fourth, so that it vitrifies. In the stone, we are accustomed to test fixation with such fire, even if no fusion were present. But that liquefaction is mystical. For it is understood together with fixation and constancy in fire.

By the fire of the bellows, which they number the seventh, we likewise melt violently, blow, and separate. Thus, it will not be of a lower grade. With it, we sometimes make flowers of antimony. Otherwise, metals are smelted by it. The same can also reverberate and calcine. In blowing strong spirits, the wind entering through the openings and vents takes its place, as also in glassworks.

The eighth differs little from the seventh. Its operation proceeds at least through fusion to lime.

The ninth is said to be used in examinations, so that it is certain regarding fixation and other proofs of quality. Therefore, in the masterwork of the stone, when the gold that has already been made must be subjected to judgment and examinations, this mode is used, but not alone. For medicinal substances are added, such as caustic waters, lead, salts, sulfur, antimony, and the rest of which one reads in Geber.

Other writers commemorate four types of fires, namely Natural, Non-natural, Contra-natural, and Elemental. They call the fire of nature internal and innate to things. They call the Non-natural (as physicians call non-natural things) serving, servile, and external, which is administered in various ways as the occasion of the task requires, such as for putrefaction through the bath in the first part of the work, but through ashes in the second. The Contra-natural fire tries and examines the matter violently, so that a judgment may be made regarding fixation. It is also mystical, and is named the violent Dragon, which burns like the fire of hell. This is prepared from Mercurial menstruum <note>a solvent or acid used in alchemy</note>, and it is inside the glass and burns more effectively than elemental fire, or that which is procured by wood and is called flaming. You will hear sometimes that coagulation and whitening are done with the most temperate heat, or artificially tempered, so that the hoped-for act may exist. Truly, the artist, by the constancy of heat and the accommodation of industry, even if it is of the first or second grade, can achieve the effect of the third. For one must not be in a hurry and the fire must not be precipitated if you wish to act knowingly and skillfully. You can calcine eggshells with violent fire. But if you act skillfully, you will achieve the same even with low heat and the intervention of vinegar. And it must be known that in that abstruse art, there is a powerfully acting menstruum within. If you wish to work importunely, and thus calcine in the art, as the common people make quicklime, it will happen to you as it does to brickmakers, who burn bricks with excessive fire and melt them so that they are like glass. Therefore, someone rightly warns that one must abstain from violent heat and sudden cold, and should tend to a moderate fire (applied from the art through its own modes), lest we incur vitrification. The slowest fire in the beginning dissolves and separates (as it is in the treatise of Peter of Zyleto), and that is compared to the heat of the ram, likewise the vernal heat, that of the hen incubating eggs, and the embryo: some have administered it through the bath: others through straw, or ash, or candles, or coals, etc. Altogether, one must begin with that which is foreign, and insist upon it for a long time, then proceed through the grades which experience confirms. (The knowledge of fires is the universal gift of doctrine). The same gentle fire produces blackness. There is nothing that extracts humidity from bodies and preserves it as well as a gentle fire, because fire attenuates natures and separates the liquid from the turbid. A gentle fire is that which magnesia (the Mercury of the Philosophers) does not flee. With whiteness, fixation succeeds. Thus, the heat should be increased so that it becomes similar to summer or lion-like heat, and continued until the mass turns into lime and becomes like burned ash. If you wish to proceed from here to red, you ought to increase the fire, and when this color appears, then at last there is a place for the strong one, which is otherwise called the fusing one. Inside, the fire of quicksilver works, which exerts in gold and silver that force which can be obtained by no external fire. For it burns and calcines them far more potently. But there is no need for more words. We want this example to be proposed to the Chemical novice, lest he think that fires are to be applied rashly in this art. One must absolutely accustom oneself to circumspect control, and not hurry, where the matter does not require it. Otherwise, harm is certain. When those who break into the art from the outside do not attend to this, they think they can do anything, anywhere.

§. 12. Infants and the insane are also deservedly excepted. As regards infants, they lack all distinct judgment of good and evil; they do what they seem to be delinquent in ignorantly and against their will. Finally, they lack choice, and thus are immune from all guilt. But with guilt denied, punishment is also denied. For the *form* of that which is inflicted upon someone, which has the rationale of punishment, is guilt, which is contracted by the transgression of the law. If this is not present, punishment also has no place. Hence Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X: *Nor was it becoming to inflict force upon such small innocence by law, etc.* The words of AMESIUS, *On Conscience, book 5, chapter 3, number 8*, bear on this: *A just punishment, he says, in its formal rationale, has respect to antecedent guilt, as an effect to its compelling or meritorious cause. As an adjunct to its similar rule from which it has measure, as a corrective act to its object to be corrected: therefore, it can have no place where no guilt has preceded.* And the Most Excellent Lord Röhrensee, Public Professor of Morals, to be honored in his teaching, in the *Disputation on the Punishment of the Innocent*, says: *There is a necessary and inseparable nexus between punishment, liability, and guilt, such as between antecedent and consequent, that with the consequent given, it is necessary that the antecedent also be given, even if the reverse does not hold.* From these things, therefore, it is most firmly concluded that infants ought to be exempted from all punishment. Wherefore, pregnant women are also not ordinarily punished, lest something be inflicted upon the innocent fetus, which it was for the mother alone to suffer.

### On the Origin of Fire-Spitting Mountains.

---

Volcanoes always originate in the following manner: a fire-throat opens at a low spot in flat terrain. The opening throws out a quantity of burning materials, which partly flow down as lava and partly ascend into the air, falling down in the form of hail. These materials form a cone, just as a molehill is formed by thrown-up earth, or a small mound is formed at the bottom of an hourglass by falling sand. The channel through which these materials pass always remains open in the center of this cone as long as the eruptions continue. If new openings form on a mountain, they are likely old fire-throats that have merely been reopened: a completely new fire always breaks out where the crust is thinnest, i. e., in the plains and valleys, not in the mountains, unless there are already old, previously opened channels there. However, the fire-spitting mountains themselves, whose materials lie one upon the other without order or firm connection, are very easily penetrated by fire.
